text:
All night, sleep fled from her bed. “The child must have a father,” she thought over and over again.

The next morning, the farmer had to go to Ekeby on her behalf and fetch Gösta Berling.

Gösta asked the taciturn man many questions, but learned nothing. Yes, the Countess had been in his house all summer. She had been well and had worked. Now a child had been born. The child was frail, but the mother would soon be well again.

Gösta asked whether the Countess knew that the marriage had been dissolved.

Yes, she knew now. She had learned of it yesterday.

And for as long as the journey lasted, Gösta alternated between fever and chills.

What did she want with him? Why had she sent for him?

He thought of their summer life up there on the shore of Löven. With jokes and games and pleasure outings, they had let the days pass, and meanwhile she had worked and suffered.

Never had he imagined the possibility of seeing her again. Ah, if only he had dared to hope! Then he would have appeared before her as a better man. What did he now have to look back upon but the usual follies?

At about eight in the evening, he arrived and was taken at once to the child’s mother. It was dim in the room. He could scarcely see her where she lay. The mistress and master of the house also came in.

Now it should be known that she, whose white face shone toward him out of the twilight, was still the highest and purest being he knew, the most beautiful soul ever to clothe itself in earthly dust. Now that he once more experienced the blessing of her presence, he would have liked to cast himself down on his knees and thank her for revealing herself to him again, but he was so overwhelmed with emotion that he could neither say nor do anything.

“Dear Countess Elisabet!” was all he exclaimed.

“Good evening, Gösta!”

She held out her hand to him, which once more seemed to have become soft and translucent. She lay silent while he struggled with his emotion.

The child’s mother was not shaken by any violently surging feelings when she saw Gösta. It merely surprised her that he seemed to attach the greatest importance to her, when he surely ought to understand that now only the child mattered.

“Gösta,” she said gently, “you must help me now, as you once promised. You know that my husband has abandoned me, so that my child has no father.”

“Yes, Countess, but surely this can be changed. Now that there is a child, the Count can certainly be forced to legalize the marriage. Be assured that I shall help the Countess!”

The Countess smiled faintly.

“Do you think I wish to force myself upon Count Dohna?”

The blood rushed to Gösta’s head. Then what did she want? What was she asking of him?

“Come here, Gösta!” she said, again holding out her hand. “You must not be angry with me for what I am about to say, but I thought that you, who are, who are…”

“A defrocked priest, a hard drinker, a Cavalier, Ebba Dohna’s murderer—I know the whole list of merits…”

“Are you angry already, Gösta?”

“I would rather the Countess did not say anything more.”

But the child’s mother continued:

“There are many women, Gösta, who would have wished to become your wife for love’s sake, but that is not how it is with me. If I loved you, I would not dare speak as I am speaking now. For my own sake, I would not wish to ask such a thing, Gösta, but, you see, for the child’s sake I can do it. You surely understand already what I intend to ask of you. It is no doubt a great humiliation for you, since I am an unmarried woman who has a child. I did not think that you might be willing to do it because you are worse than others—though yes! I thought of that too. But chiefly I thought that you might be willing to do it because you are good, Gösta, because you are a hero and can sacrifice yourself. But perhaps it is asking too much. Such a thing may be impossible for a man. If you despise me too much, if it is too repugnant to you to be named as the father of another man’s child, then just say so! I shall not be angry. I understand that this is asking too much, but the child is so ill, Gösta. It is so cruel that at his baptism the name of his mother’s husband cannot be given.”

He, who listened to her, felt the same as he had on that spring day when he had been compelled to put her ashore and abandon her to her fate. Now he had to help her destroy her future, her entire future. He, who loved her, had to do it.

“I will do whatever the Countess wishes,” he said.

The next day, he spoke with the dean in Bro, for Bro is the mother parish of Svartsjö, and the banns had to be taken out there.

The good old dean was moved by his story and promised to take upon himself all responsibility regarding the marriage guardian and the like.

“Yes,” he said, “you must help her, Gösta, you must. Otherwise she might go mad. She believes she has harmed the child by depriving him of his position in life. That woman has an exceedingly sensitive conscience.”

“But I know that I shall make her unhappy,” Gösta burst out.

“You most certainly must not do that, Gösta. You must become a sober-minded man now, with a wife and child to provide for.”

Meanwhile, the dean was to go down to Svartsjö and speak with both the curate and the judge. The outcome of it all was that on the following Sunday, the first of September, the banns of marriage between Gösta Berling and Elisabet von Thurn were proclaimed in Svartsjö.

Then the child’s mother was conveyed with the greatest care to Ekeby, and there the child was baptized.

The dean then spoke with her and told her that she could still reverse her decision to marry a man such as Gösta Berling. Surely she ought to write to her father first.

“I cannot change my mind,” she said. “Suppose my child were to die before he had been given a father!”

By the time the third day of the banns came, the child’s mother had already been well and out of bed for several days. In the afternoon, the dean came to Ekeby and married her to Gösta Berling. But no one thought of this as a wedding. No guests had been invited. They were merely providing the child with a father, nothing else.

The child’s mother shone with a quiet joy, as though she had attained a great goal in life. The bridegroom was sorrowful. He thought of how she was throwing away her future in a marriage to him. With horror, he realized that he scarcely existed for her at all. All her thoughts were with the child.
